newsitem.title: USA: U.S. analysts see glowing Q4 bank earnings.
newsitem.headline: U.S. analysts see glowing Q4 bank earnings.

text.p: Handsome fourth quarter earnings should cheer investors in U.S. bank stocks, as banks report higher profits on fee income and on a modest improvement in their traditional lending business, analysts said.

Anthony Davis, an analyst at Dean Witter Reynolds, said that excluding a couple of banks in unusual circumstances, earnings for the group will be up about 13 or 14 percent year-over-year -- double the pace of the Standard & Poor's 500.
The bank earnings season begins January 13.
George Salem, analyst at Gerard Klauer Mattison, said in a recent research report that the fourth quarter should see the same strong momentum as previous quarters of 1996.

Median earnings per share growth should be 13 percent, boosted by several factors, Salem said. He cited healthy loan growth, especially from consumers, flat to slightly higher interest margins, and "quite decent" non-interest income.

Also contributing will be low charge-offs despite moderately higher credit card losses, while expenses rose at only a low single-digit rate. Heavy stock buybacks will also help per share earnings, he said.
One of the few negative factors will be slightly lower trading revenues, he said.
Prudential Securities analyst Ruchi Madan said in a recent report she expects "solid earnings growth," averaging 10 to 12 percent higher for a group of regional banks.
Madan said loan growth should be similar to the third quarter, while net interest margins expand slightly.

Federal Reserve data shows industry-wide loan growth continued to be about six percent in the fourth quarter from a year ago, unchanged from the third quarter, but below the seven to eight percent growth earlier this year, she said.
Fee income should be strong, particularly in the capital markets area, Madan aid.
Of the 14 bank stocks Salem tracks, he expects only one, J.P. Morgan & Co Inc, to show a decline in earnings, to $1.60 per share from $1.80 a year ago.

Salem said Morgan's corporate finance and trading revenues did well in October, but November was weak and December was hurt by seasonal factors. As an investment bank, its business mix makes it more vulnerable to those sectors.

One factor that has marred the outlook for bank stocks for some time is the rise in delinquent credit card debt. During all of 1996, quarterly earnings reports have been carefully combed over for trends in that area.
Salem, one of the first to raise an alarm on the subject, said in his latest report that overall earnings should not be hurt despite new highs in credit card losses.

Davis at Dean Witter said net charge-offs for card loans will be in the 4.90 to 4.95 percent range, compared to 4.75 percent in the third quarter. Overall loan charge-offs should be in the 0.55 to 0.60 percent area compared to 0.56 percent in the third quarter, he said.
But a report just before Christmas from research firm Veribanc Inc took a more somber outlook, noting that seriously delinquent credit card debt exceeded $4 billion at the end of the third quarter.
The report said credit card debt more than 90 days past due or placed in non-accrual status had crept up to 1.83 percent of card debt in bank loan portfolios from 1.68 percent in the second quarter.
Noting that personal bankruptcies have soared, Veribanc said non-credit card consumer installment debt has also deteriorated.
((-- New York Newsdesk 212 859-1732))
